papers.paper: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

questions.question: What kind of intermediate steps does chain-of-thought prompting generate?
questions.answer: (1) First, producing a chain of thought, in principle, allows models to decompose multi-step problems into intermediate steps, which means that additional computation can be allo-cated to problems that require more reasoning steps.

source_quotes.source_quote: (1) First, producing a chain of thought, in principle, allows models to decompose multi-step problems into intermediate steps, which means that additional computation can be allo-cated to problems that require more reasoning steps.

questions.question: What scale of language models does the paper say chain-of-thought prompting works with?
questions.answer: Notably, chain of thought prompting does better than standard prompting only at the scale of ∼100B parameters; models of smaller scale produced fluent but illogical chains of thought, leading to lower performance than standard prompting.

source_quotes.source_quote: Notably, chain of thought prompting does better than standard prompting only at the scale of ∼100B parameters; models of smaller scale produced fluent but illogical chains of thought, leading to lower performance than standard prompting.

questions.question: Which arithmetic reasoning benchmark is named in the paper?
questions.answer: Following both the Math Word Problem Repos-itory (Koncel-Kedziorski et al., 2016), and more-recent benchmarks (Cobbe et al., 2021), we consider the following six datasets: (1) SingleOp (Roy et al., 2015), (2) SingleEq (Koncel-Kedziorski et al., 2015), (3) AddSub (Hosseini et al., 2014), (4) ASDiv (Miao et al., 2020), (5) MultiArith (Roy & Roth, 2015), and (6) GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021).
